text: Cassini's final trajectory made a hit on Enceladus a real possibility. After thirteen years around Saturn, its path could have intersected that moon's orbit, and a collision could transfer Earth contaminants into an ocean that might support life. Enceladus ejects icy plumes and has a subsurface ocean, making it a strong candidate for habitability studies. Deorbiting it into Saturn's upper atmosphere destroyed the probe instead of letting it drift, bounce, or be deflected back to hit the moon again. If it had hit Enceladus at low speed, fragments or residual materials could contaminate the surface or the plume region. That was the end-of-mission biosafety reason.

When you skate, one leg does the pushing while the other stays on the deck. The pushing leg has to generate the force, so the muscles along that side are working through a big range of motion. The hip flexor, adductors, and quadriceps on that side get stretched out and then contract hard with every kick. That combination of stretching under load and repeated force build up fatigue in the muscles and the joints around the hip and knee.

The other leg, the one you ask about, is not completely passive. It has to keep the board level and stable, which means the muscles on that side are working isometrically to hold the posture. Over time the small constant tension in those muscles can become a dull, tired ache. That is different from the sharp strain on the pushing side.

Pain in the stationary leg usually shows up when skating for a long time or when the pushing leg has taken most of the load. It is a common complaint among people who skate for extended periods, especially if they have one-sided technique. If the aching persists, changing the stance, alternating the pushing leg more often, and warming up the muscles before and after skating can reduce it.

The label points to ancestral ties to Africa, not current residence or recent migration. For much of U.S. history, the largest source of enslaved people was West and Central Africa, with groups such as Igbo, Yoruba, Fon, Ashanti and Mandinka among others, so the connection is historical rather than contemporary. Most Black Americans today were born in the U.S. or arrived from places like Jamaica, Haiti or Brazil, but their families generally carry African roots. That is what makes them African Americans in the ethnic sense. The term also works as a national and cultural identifier: Black Americans share a history shaped by slavery, segregation, migration from the South to northern and western cities, and ongoing cultural exchange with Africa. It is not a statement that everyone can trace a family to a specific village; many family records are missing or incomplete. In practice, “African American” is used because African descent is central to that group’s identity, even when no individual is themselves an African-born person. The hyphenated “Afro-American” foregrounds the cultural and continental association, while the standard U.S. term is African American. You do not need to be born in Africa to belong to the broader African diaspora.

The word bad hides a mix of harms: acute effects, chronic changes, and risk of overdose, especially when a drug is powerful but not self-limiting. A drug can give intense pleasure without an immediate adverse effect in the sense that the user feels good; that only changes what can go wrong later. If it hits the reward pathways hard enough to produce euphoria, the nervous system usually compensates. With opioids, activation of mu receptors reduces pain signals and increases pleasure through endogenous opioid pathways, but with regular use the brain reduces its own sensitivity, so the same dose produces less effect. That is tolerance. Tolerance pushes people to take more, which increases overdose risk because the ceiling for pleasure often does not match the ceiling for depression of breathing. Cocaine and amphetamines work differently, by blocking or triggering dopamine reuptake and release; the high comes from a sharp rise in dopamine signaling. With repeated use the postsynaptic cells adapt, making the baseline feel worse, so the next dose is needed to feel normal. This is not merely a habit. It is a measurable change in how the brain processes reward, which explains why many users cannot stop even when they do not want to.

A hypothetical zero-adverse-effect euphoric still has to perturb the reward system. If it leaves the system unchanged, the euphoria would be faint or short; if it leaves strong adaptation, chronic use changes behavior, motivation and health. That is why bad is not absolute. Some drugs are far safer than others, and many people use some substances without obvious harm, but the same mechanisms that make a drug rewarding are the same mechanisms that drive dependence and overdose when used repeatedly or at high dose. No drug is bad in every case. Dose, frequency, route and individual physiology decide a lot. A drug could be self-limiting or only mildly perturbing, but then it may not be very euphoric. If it is intense and repeatable, chronic use tends to create tolerance, craving, and a lowered baseline. Withdrawal is not proof a drug is inherently bad, but it is evidence the body has remodeled itself. If a drug gives no withdrawal, users may still crave it because reward signals have changed and drive the desire for another dose. That does not make every use harmful, but it explains why zero adverse effects are hard to combine with intense euphoria.

Hi,

What you're feeling is real, and I think this is not a standard tension headache. In a long, low-light mall day, the combination of standing still, poor posture and sustained eye focus can make the neck and upper-back muscles hold on and send dull, aching signals, which some people experience as a weird physical pressure. Another possibility is mild hyperventilation or dehydration, but the postural tension one fits better.

All the best,

A friend

Hey Sam,
You were not making a factual error. Repeating a word five times puts it in your head so you keep hearing its sound pattern. Milk rhymes with silk, and your brother asked a question right after the repetition. Your brain grabbed the sounding word instead of the factual answer. That is a kind of mental set. Cows drink water; milk is what they give, not what they consume. You said milk because the rhyming pair was on the tip of your tongue and the rhythm carried you along. Your brother did not test knowledge, he just got you caught in the repetition. It is not a sign you do not know what cows drink. It means the repetition opened an association channel and your brain followed it. If you were tired or distracted, the slip would be easier. So treat it as a slip.
All the best,
Alex

Hi Sam,

Buy a house for what you want it for, not for the market. If it is to live in, prioritize room, street, commute and the things that will make a small change hard to undo, because those are the ones that will bother you later. If you are buying to rent out, focus on location, demand and how easily the place will stay occupied, and keep repair costs in mind, not just the purchase price.

Before you commit, check the title and the surveys, and don't assume the seller has said everything. Get a mortgage pre-approval first, and remember it can change between that and the day you buy. Budget for stamp duty, legal fees, moving and a cushion for repairs. A cheap house with hidden problems costs more in the end.

When you find something that looks right, make an offer with a survey and finance condition, not unconditional unless you are certain. If the seller has other buyers, say your offer, not your whole financial position. A house that needs work may be cheaper now, but the price should reflect that. Also, ask what has changed in the house since it was built.

Take time on the contract and any building issues. Do not sign because of pressure.

Regards,
Sam

Hi Sam

The short version is: a 3-in-1 has to be all things to all people, so it's usually a compromise on every front. A real shampoo is a surfactant system balanced for your scalp; a real conditioner has conditioning agents and a slight cationic charge to reduce friction and frizz; a real body wash is a gentler, more alkaline-leaning cleanser for skin. A single bottle trying to be all of these will lean toward the shampoo behavior, leaving you with a weak conditioner and a harsh-enough body wash for skin. That's exactly why 3-in-1 feels like weak conditioner on your hair - the conditioning component is diluted to make room for body-wash chemistry.

The 2-in-1 is the same logic one step closer: you get real shampoo plus some conditioning agent, but you never get the full strength of a standalone conditioner, because the two chemistries compete for the same pH and foaming profile.

So the practical difference is not "three products" in one, it's a middle-of-the-road formula. Fine if you're traveling, or you don't mind your conditioner being a hint. If you're sensitive or you actually use all three, the separate bottles give you much more targeted performance.

Let me know if you want brand names to test.

All the best,
Alex

Hi Mark

We measure it with GPS. A geodetic network of fixed reference marks on each plate records positions in an Earth centered coordinate frame. By comparing the same marks days, months and years apart, we get velocities. The frame is ITRF or equivalent, built from many GPS and VLBI stations, and it smooths the signal. VLBI ties into this too: radio telescopes lock onto quasars and let the frame stay stable over long baselines.

What the data actually show is motion of roughly a few centimetres per year. The North American plate drifts about 2 cm per year, but relative velocities between plates can be much larger. GPS gives the present rate; geology gives the long term average by dating rock formations and seafloor stripes. The same idea applies to ocean plates; the rate comes from tracking their drift relative to the reference frame. You can see the motion directly in the station data instead of inferring it from rocks.

For the speed question, satellite tracking and fixed surveys provide the present day geodetic rate. The result comes from a repeatable network, and errors are dominated by atmospheric effects. That is how you get the velocity.

Best regards,
Alex

Inbreeding raises homozygosity, which is the share of an individual's genome where both gene copies are identical. Because close relatives share recent ancestors, their children are more likely to inherit two copies of the same rare harmful recessive allele. Recessive deleterious alleles usually stay hidden when only one copy is present, but when a child gets two, the harmful trait can show up, and some of those traits affect brain development and therefore cognition. So the lower IQ is not a new bad mutation; it is the chance that an existing harmful recessive gene gets paired with its matching copy.

The effect is probabilistic and scales with how closely related the parents are. The science is straightforward genetics: inbreeding does not make genes worse, it makes existing recessive problems much more likely to surface in the offspring.

Pain is not simply a report of tissue damage. The brain weighs the meaning of the injury as well as the signal from the body. An injury to the arm often seems less painful or less serious because it is on a limb away from the trunk. It usually spares major organs and core movement, and it is easier to see and treat. The person can feel it is manageable, so they react less strongly.

The arm also contains muscles and soft tissue that can absorb a blow, while many other areas, like the face or lower legs, have denser nerve endings and thinner skin over bone. If the same wound is on a joint, tendon or hand, the perceived pain can be much higher. Location matters because the body treats a limb injury as less of an emergency than a torso or head injury, and the emotional reaction changes how painful the wound feels.

Carbon monoxide is the quiet killer, and that's the part that matters most here. It is invisible and has no smell, so you do not notice it until it is already building up. The real problem is in the blood. Red blood cells carry oxygen using hemoglobin. Oxygen binds to hemoglobin, but carbon monoxide grabs the same sites and does not let go. The affinity difference is about 250 times higher for carbon monoxide than oxygen, so once carbon monoxide sits on hemoglobin, oxygen struggles to take its place. The blood carries less oxygen around the body, and organs start to suffocate. Carbon dioxide does not do this to healthy blood, and you already know the other side of the exchange: lungs take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide. So when air gets full of carbon dioxide you breathe it out and move on. That is why the contrast with carbon monoxide is so dangerous: one gas leaves, the other stays. A common situation is a fire. Burning fuel that is starved of oxygen gives off carbon monoxide. A small fire in a room can fill the space with it before anyone notices, and that is the everyday warning that keeps coming up in this discussion.

When the airplane makes a sudden stop or hits the ground, our bodies keep moving because of inertia. The brace position controls that forward motion so we do not crash into the seat back, overhead bins, or the seat ahead of us. A new passenger does not need to become an expert; they only need to know the simple movements.

Before a predicted impact, crew will tell you to brace. You sit as close to the seat back as possible, bend your knees, keep your head low and close to your knees if space allows, and use your arms and hands to shield your face and neck. The position is not meant to make the impact less severe for the airplane; it makes the impact easier for your body. It helps keep the neck from whiplash, reduces the chance that the head will strike hard, and keeps the arms and hands from flailing into other passengers or equipment. Holding it through the impact and for a short time after can also keep you from being jarred when the aircraft jolts again. That small discipline is a basic safety habit that reduces injuries during emergency landings.

Businesses we recognize today mostly depend on industrial technologies and modern supply chains, so very few have survived from before that era. Early companies often operated within small local markets and relied on handcraft, animal power and short-distance trade. Some, such as the Dutch East India Company and the English East India Company, were huge chartered firms, but they were eventually dissolved or transformed. Most older firms disappeared through bankruptcy, mergers or being absorbed into larger groups, and the original name was lost. Many were also small local enterprises, not known outside their region.

I have come to believe the dealer’s lower rate is only a line item, separate from the total cost. A dealership can quote a lower APR and still cost more because you pay a larger loan balance and dealer-imposed charges. The advertised rate measures lender interest only. It does not capture dealership charges added to the price or the monthly payment.

Suppose a buyer finances $30,000 over 60 months. At 4.0% APR the interest is roughly $3,100. At a 6.5% bank APR it is roughly $5,200. The dealer’s lower rate looks better by about $2,000, but that gap shrinks quickly once the dealer fees are counted. A $750 documentation fee, a $1,000 market adjustment, $900 for GAP coverage, and $1,100 for an extended service plan add nearly $3,750, which outweighs the interest savings. The bank can end up cheaper even at the higher headline rate.

When I looked at financing last year, the dealer offered 2.9% APR on a new car, but it came with a $1,250 fees bundle and a tire and wheel package. The bank’s 5.2% loan had a small origination fee and no mandatory extras. I could put down more money and shorten the term, which cut the principal and the total interest. The lower dealer rate left room for other charges.

The dealer’s low rate is often a bargaining chip. It may apply only to certain trims, a longer term, or a specific model, while the dealership adds charges for documentation, market adjustment, insurance and warranties. A bank does not bundle those charges and lets the buyer choose the down payment and term. The buyer should compare the out-the-door total, and treat the APR as just one input. If the dealer’s lower rate comes with thousands in fees, the bank’s higher rate can still mean the smaller bill.

The difference is the package and what the buyer must buy. A $1,000 advertising fee or dealer prep charge can erase the rate advantage in a few months. I keep a simple rule: I take the same loan amount and term the dealer proposes, get a matching bank quote, and add every fee line by line. A low APR is easy to compare on paper, but the dealership package is where the real difference appears. I compare the payment amount and the total fees too, since a low rate can mask expensive add-ons.

I support legalizing marijuana at the state level. It lets Colorado, California, New York and Missouri choose tax rates, licensing rules and age limits without waiting on Congress. Colorado was one of the first recreational states in 2012; California followed in 2016 and has built out a large regulated market, while Missouri entered the recreational list later, in 2022. The patchwork can feel unfair: you can be legal in one state and still have to cross the line to get the same plant that used to be banned everywhere. Medical marijuana programs also matter because they give chronic pain and epilepsy patients access to what actually helps them. The Schedule I label keeps creating headaches for banks and employers. It also gives states real revenue, not just permission slips, and helps fund programs. I think that flexibility is what makes state legalization actually work for ordinary people.

My heart, not a spark, is where I understood the body makes electricity. The real trick is ion gradients. In a nerve cell, the sodium-potassium pump moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in, creating charge separation. That gradient lets sodium flood in through voltage-gated channels, flipping membrane potential in milliseconds. This isn't stored charge; it is moving ions doing chemical work that becomes voltage. So the body's electricity is ion transport, not magic. What I find hard to believe is how many sodium pumps running at once make measurable current. It is physiology, not mysticism.

I don't mind sampling when the old record gets chopped up and made to fit a new key and tempo, and I do mind when someone just drops a four-second hook they've heard a thousand times on the radio. That's the split. A recognizable fragment is easy; the craft is in making a broken piece of an older song become part of a new composition rather than just wearing a recognizable badge.

Take The Avalanches. They went through hundreds of records to make the beats for *Here, Come On*. A lot of those old recordings were 78s or early LPs, and instead of playing the original songs as-is, they looped a few bars, chopped the drum hits, and pitched them into new keys. The result sounds like one song, not a mixtape of old songs stitched together. J Dilla did the same move with even fewer samples and a looser feel; he'd take a short melodic fragment and swing it into a new groove. That's the technique I care about: the sample stops being a reference and becomes raw material.

I think people get hung up on copyright and whether the sample is "too famous." That matters for releases, but it's not the interesting part. The interesting part is the transformation. You can have a sample that is technically clear and legally shaky, and it can still sound great. I've worked on a track, called Astronomical, where I used a fragment from an old R&B record and stretched it across two minutes of a new song. The original was a slow waltz; I cut the melody into short pieces and re-timed them. The listener might recognize the old song, but the new piece has its own shape. If the sample still feels like the original song in disguise, I've failed.

I also get frustrated with samples used to fill dead space in a verse. That's a filler sample. It doesn't carry the beat or the melody; it just occupies a gap, and the new song needs it to avoid silence. The difference is whether the sample is doing real structural work. When I cut a vocal loop from an old record, I want that loop to drive the rhythm. When I take a bass fragment from an older soul record and pitch it down into a new key, that fragment becomes the foundation of the section.

There's another thing I don't like: using a sample in the original tempo and key, with nothing new. That's not lazy in the sense of doing no work, but it's a missed chance. The whole point of sampling older songs is that you are borrowing the texture of the past, not copying the old song note for note. I'd rather see the sample bent, chopped, and re-pitched so the older music is made to serve the new idea.

I'm also curious about what counts as a recognizable sample and what doesn't. Some artists use a fragment so short and so distorted that the original is barely there, while others use a hook that screams "here's the old song." I prefer the first approach. If you can tell immediately which older song a sample came from, you're just paying homage. If you have to listen twice, the sample has been properly absorbed.

That's where the real work happens. The older record stops being itself and becomes the floor of the new composition. I'd rather have a sample I can't immediately place than one that's a recognizable clip. The old song's ghost is still in there, but it's no longer a quote; it's a material. That's the part I find worth doing.

I keep seeing that old myth that our heads are just bags of liquid, and when you get a bad headache it’s because your brain is swelling in your skull. But that’s not how the pain actually works. What’s happening is irritation and inflammation in the pain-sensitive blood vessels and membranes around the brain, not the brain tissue itself. In migraines especially, those vessels go through changes that can be measured, and that’s the main source of the aching.

We still can't say whether the food is good because we never got to eat. We got there at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday and picked this place for a 10 p.m. show in the same hotel, expecting it to be easy. Their digital waitlist was completely useless. We put our names in, then were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We paid, but stood there till 8:40 p.m. before someone said we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15 p.m. Just two of us, and they offered no way to avoid a very long wait. If a wait can stretch that far past payment, say so up front instead of letting people lose the evening. Absolute disaster. Zero stars, if that was even an option.

No line Friday at about 4:30. Two plates came to about $130. I thought before going it’d be around steakhouse prices, but afterward I realized the buffet actually ran a bit above that. No steak, which at that price was disappointing. Meat side had lamb, prime rib, chicken, all things I get at other Vegas buffets for considerably less.

The seafood corner had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Crab legs are everywhere in Vegas, but the rock crab claws are the one thing I hadn’t seen at other places. No crab crackers. Staff said wooden mallets, but our table was pressed right up to the next one, so I didn’t want to smash shells over our neighbors. Ended up eating just the legs.

The Asian side wasn’t all that distinctive; it brought the Rampart Casino buffet to mind, which is the comparison I keep making. Dessert was gelato and pastries with fresh juices, though I didn’t taste any of those. I’d call the whole thing acceptable but overpriced for what it gives you. If you’re inclined to try it, do it once if you can get there without waiting. If there’s a queue, I’d probably think again.

It gets four stars; I keep it. The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. That happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I type fast without looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had pulled off a keycap and found them: brown tactile switches, a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle. Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I would have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I now tap the space bar a little closer to the middle.

I’ve gone to Vegas most of my life. Mostly because I was too young to do the gambling part. Well, the under-21 side of it, which means I’ve seen a lot of shows before I could gamble. I finally caught Le Rêve at the Wynn, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe a little worse than mixed.

The good stuff: the circular stage is actually clever. You look down into it, so from almost any seat you get a decent view. That’s rare for Vegas, and the view stays good from nearly every seat. Some acts are really good, like the strength stuff, aerialists, and divers. Those people are proper athletes. It also brings to mind Cirque du Soleil. Not a rip-off, just if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen similar feats, probably done with more clarity.

Clarity is the issue. What’s the story? I still don’t know. Is there a dream? A guy? Water? It feels like a pile of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s actually saying. Also, too much is happening at once. Too many people, elements, and stacked wow moments. A more restrained show would land harder. It feels like the usual Vegas spectacle mindset, where more must be better, so they crammed in everything.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, there’s a $99 deal instead of the normal $125. That helps for people staying at the hotel. Would I go again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it twice. Outside of a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. Some friends liked it, so if you haven’t seen it, maybe try it. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

Roughly two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by telephone. They never arrived because the sales representative got the delivery address wrong. Her handwritten 7 was read as a 1. Our address was 5407, but the package went to 5401. The residents there took it to the local UPS store to be returned. After that, it disappeared and was never seen or heard from again. We found out several weeks later. During the dispute we placed an additional order for two shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two. The owner took over and said he would not issue a refund until the shirts were returned, after admitting the shipment had gone to the wrong address. He also put some of the blame on us because we had not been friendly enough to the residents at 5401, four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company, and eventually got the credit.
